t.6.67.1: Hearing that Makarākṣa had been slain, Rāvaṇa, conqueror in battle, then, enraged, commanded his son Indrajit to go into battle.
t.6.67.2: O hero, slay the two mighty brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa! Whether unseen or seen, you are in every way superior in strength.
t.6.67.3: You conquer in battle even Indra, whose deeds are matchless; how much more, then, once you have seen the two men, will you not slay them in battle?
t.6.67.4: Thus addressed by the lord of the rākṣasas, Indrajit accepted his father's words and, at the place of sacrifice, duly made offerings into the fire according to the prescribed rites.
t.6.67.5: And as he was offering oblations into the fire there, rākṣasī women wearing red turbans came in agitation to the place where Rāvaṇi was.
t.6.67.7: Having strewn arrow-shafts all around the fire on every side, he seized by the throat a living goat that was entirely black.
t.6.67.6: Weapons served as the śara-reed leaves, and vibhītaka wood as the kindling sticks; there were red garments, and likewise a ladle made of black iron.
t.6.67.8: From the fire, kindled by oblations of caru, smokeless and blazing with great flames, there arose those signs, and they foretold victory.
t.6.67.9: With flames whirling toward the right and gleaming like molten gold, Pāvaka, the fire-god, rising up of his own accord, received that oblation.
t.6.67.10: Having made offerings into the fire and then having satisfied the gods, Dānavas and Rākṣasas, he mounted his splendid, excellent chariot, which had the power of becoming invisible.
t.6.67.11: Furnished with four horses and with sharpened arrows, he, his mighty bow strung, shone forth upon that most excellent chariot.
t.6.67.12: Blazing with splendour in its form and furnished with trappings of refined gold, that chariot was richly adorned with arrows and with full-moon and half-moon ornaments.
t.6.67.14: Protected by that sun-like chariot and by the Brahmāstra, Rāvaṇi, of exceedingly great strength, became unassailable.
t.6.67.13: Indrajit's banner, with its great staff of jāmbūnada gold and adorned with lapis lazuli, was like a blazing fire.
t.6.67.15: Having sallied forth from the city, Indrajit, victorious in battle, made offerings into the fire with rākṣasa mantras and, having become invisible, spoke.
t.6.67.17: "Having rid the earth of monkeys and slain Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa, I shall bring about the greatest delight." Having said this, he vanished.
t.6.67.16: Today, having slain in battle those two who have falsely gone forth as ascetics into the forest, I shall give my father Rāvaṇa a victory greater than any won in war.
t.6.67.18: Then the fierce enemy of Indra, enraged and urged on by Daśagrīva, rushed forward in battle with his sharp bow and iron arrows.
t.6.67.19: He beheld the two mighty heroes standing amid the vānaras, like a pair of three-headed serpents, loosing nets of arrows.
t.6.67.20: Thinking, "These are those two," he strung his bow and covered them with streams of arrows, like a rain-cloud pouring down rain.
t.6.67.21: But he, having risen into the sky with his chariot, and staying beyond the range of sight, pierced Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with sharpened arrows.
t.6.67.22: Those two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, overwhelmed by the force of his arrows, fitted arrows to their bows and invoked a divine weapon.
t.6.67.23: The two mighty ones, resembling gods, covered the sky with nets of arrows and with their weapons, yet they could not touch him at all with their arrows.
t.6.67.24: For he created a darkness of smoke, covering the sky, and the glorious one, enveloped in a gloom of mist, hid the directions from view.
t.6.67.25: As he moved about, neither the twang of his bowstring against the arm-guard nor the sound of chariot-rims and hooves was heard, nor was his form visible.
t.6.67.26: In the dense, gloomy darkness, the mighty-armed one poured down what seemed a wondrous rain of arrows, with showers of nārāca shafts.
t.6.67.27: Enraged in battle, Rāvaṇi, who had been granted a boon, pierced Rāma deeply in all his limbs with arrows resembling the sun.
t.6.67.28: Those two tigers among men, though being struck by iron arrows like two mountains pelted by torrents of rain, released sharp arrows fitted with golden feathers.
t.6.67.30: Though grievously harassed by the flood of arrows, the two best of men cut down those falling shafts with many broad-headed bhalla arrows.
t.6.67.29: Reaching Rāvaṇi in the sky, those heron-feathered flying shafts cut into him and fell to the earth, drenched in blood.
t.6.67.31: Wherever the two of them saw the sharp arrows falling, from there and there the two sons of Daśaratha released a supreme missile.
t.6.67.32: But Rāvaṇi, a peerless chariot-warrior swift in wielding his weapons, rushing in his chariot through all the quarters, pierced those two sons of Daśaratha with sharpened arrows.
t.6.67.33: Pierced deeply by him with gold-feathered, close-packed arrows, those two heroes, the sons of Daśaratha, looked like two kiṃśuka trees in full bloom.
t.6.67.34: No one knew his movement, nor his form, his bow or his arrows, nor was anything else of him perceived, as with the sun when the clouds gather and engulf it.
t.6.67.35: Pierced and struck down by him, the monkeys there, by the hundreds, became lifeless and fell upon the surface of the earth.
t.6.67.36: But Lakṣmaṇa, greatly enraged, spoke these words to his brother: "I shall employ the Brāhma weapon for the slaying of all the Rākṣasas."
t.6.67.37: Then Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa, who bore auspicious marks: "For the sake of one alone, you ought not to slay the rākṣasas upon the earth."
t.6.67.38: You ought not to slay here one who is not fighting, one who is hidden, one who stands with joined palms, one who has come for refuge, one who is fleeing, or one who is off his guard.
t.6.67.39: O mighty one, we two shall strive for the slaying of this one alone, and we shall direct at him swift and mighty missiles that are like venomous serpents.
t.6.67.40: The leaders of the vānara troops, once they have seen him, will forcibly slay that wily, base rākṣasa whose chariot is hidden from sight.
t.6.67.41: Even if he should enter the earth, or heaven, or Rasātala, or the expanse of the sky, even though hidden thus, he will be burned by my weapons and fall lifeless upon the surface of the earth.
t.6.67.42: Having spoken these words, the great-souled foremost hero of the Raghus, surrounded by the bull-like monkeys, then quickly looked out, great-souled one that he was, for the slaying of that fierce one of cruel deeds.
